title: Uposatha
hook: on moon days lay people may keep eight precepts for a day and a night (AN 8.41)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pamada, a clear mind, the fifth precept, the guard at the gate. Your line was keep the mind clear. Did you catch the moment something started to cloud you? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

Go to a temple in Sri Lanka or Thailand on the night of a full moon and you may see something unusual. People dressed all in white, lay people, not monks, staying the whole day and into the night. They skip dinner. They leave the jewelry and the perfume at home. Nobody's watching a game on their phone. They're not monks and they aren't trying to become monks. For one day and one night, they're living a little closer to how monks live. It happens every week or so, following the moon. Today's word is that day.
screen: `WHITE CLOTHES, A FULL MOON.` → `NOT MONKS, BUT CLOSE.` → `ONE DAY AND ONE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Uposatha. It's the observance day, following the phases of the moon: the full moon, the new moon, and in many places the half moons in between. So it comes about once a week. On uposatha days, lay people may take eight precepts instead of five. Precept three becomes complete celibacy for the day. Then three more are added. Not eating after noon. No dancing, singing, music or shows, and no garlands, perfumes or makeup. And no high or luxurious beds: you sleep on something simple. A discourse in the Numerical Discourses lays out these eight, and it has a beautiful way of framing them. For each precept, the lay follower reflects: the arahants, the fully awakened ones, keep this as long as they live. Today, for this one night and day, I'll keep it too, following their example. So it isn't a penance. It's a rehearsal, a day of borrowing a freer life. The Vinaya tells how the gatherings began. Other religious groups met on these moon days to teach, and people came to listen. King Bimbisara noticed, and suggested that the Buddha's followers gather too. So the monks began meeting on moon days, and later in the same chapter they are told to recite their monastic rules together, as they still do every two weeks. Lay people come to the temple, listen to teaching, sit, and keep their eight precepts. A day kept apart: white clothes, an empty plate after noon, a plain mat, and the moon.
screen: `A MOON DAY, ABOUT ONCE A WEEK.` · `EIGHT PRECEPTS FOR A DAY AND NIGHT.` · `FOLLOWING THE ARAHANTS' EXAMPLE.` · `A KING, MOON DAYS, THE MONKS GATHER.` · then, large: `A DAY KEPT APART.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Picture the temple courtyard on a full-moon night: white clothes, a quiet crowd, the moon coming up over the roof. Now picture one day in your own life kept a little apart. What would you set down for it? Maybe the evening snack, the music, the scrolling. You don't have to decide anything now. Just feel what a simpler day might be like. After the bell, look up when the next full moon is. The bell holds the time.
Uposatha. The observance day on the full moon, the new moon and the half moons, when lay people may keep eight precepts for a day and a night.
Your line: a day kept apart. Today, find out when the next full moon is, and put it in your calendar, with one small thing you'll set down that day. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: On uposatha days, Theravada lay Buddhists who keep the day go to the temple, often dressed in white, take the eight precepts, listen to teaching and meditate; monks gather every two weeks to recite their monastic rules.

match.prompt: match the piece of the uposatha day.
pairs: one of the three added precepts
the example lay people follow for a day
the king who suggested moon-day gatherings

myth: on uposatha, lay people become monks for the day
they stay lay people; they keep eight precepts for one day and night.
the eight precepts include not eating after noon
along with celibacy for the day, no entertainment or adornment, and simple beds.
the moon-day gatherings began with a king's suggestion
the Vinaya says King Bimbisara proposed that the Buddha's followers gather on those days too.

fork.setup: you're keeping eight precepts for the day. it's 3 p.m. and a friend offers you a slice of cake. what does the uposatha day ask?
options: thank them and save it for tomorrow.
fork.reveal: the sixth precept is not eating after noon. one way to keep the day is to save the gift for the next morning.

original.note: Pali: the observance day, kept on the moon days.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Buddhist sabbath with strict rules.
what it means: a moon day when lay people borrow a simpler life, keeping eight precepts for a day and a night.
what a scholar hears: AN 8.41 calls it the uposatha 'with eight factors', modeled on the arahants; the Vinaya's Mahavagga says King Bimbisara suggested the moon-day gatherings.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.41 (Uposatha Sutta), the eight-factored uposatha
Vinaya, Mahavagga II.1, Bimbisara and the uposatha gathering

notes: The eight precepts and the reflection on following the arahants' example for a night and a day are paraphrased from AN 8.41; confirm.
Bimbisara's suggestion (Vinaya Mahavagga II.1) and the fortnightly patimokkha recitation should be checked.
The Sanskrit etymology (upavasatha, the Vedic fast day) was cut from voice, myth, original and trapdoor: no cited text gives it.
Uposatha frequency (full, new and half moons) varies by country and tradition.

Editor review 2026-10-01: removed the Vedic etymology (not in any cited source) everywhere and replaced that myth with Bimbisara's suggestion from the Vinaya; retold the Vinaya origin more exactly (other groups met and taught on moon days); swapped the empty closing uplift for a concrete image; softened 'many' claims.
